paper.title_en: Dynamical flattening of halo density cusps by Q-ball dark matter
paper.abstract_en: Cold, collisionless dark matter successfully explains a wide range of observations, including the formation of large-scale structure. Nevertheless, tensions remain on small, galactic scales, most notably the cusp-core, or inner-mass-deficit, problem and the diversity of inner rotation-curve shapes and central densities at fixed halo mass. These observations suggest that additional dark-sector physics may affect the inner structure of halos, although no generally accepted explanation has yet emerged. Here, making use of a toy but representative model, we investigate how interacting dark-matter Q-balls -- non-topological solitons stabilized by a conserved charge -- modify halo centers and generate a diversity of inner profiles. Our calculations include merger-induced mass and kinetic-energy losses, elastic heat transport, and the gravitational readjustment of the halo; flattening and later recontraction can both occur. Produced in the early Universe in the dark sector, these Q-balls grow in the dense central regions of halos, while their interaction cross section decreases as the soliton mass increases. This process operates preferentially in halo centers, converting part of the rest-mass energy stored in massive Q-balls into relativistic dark-sector particles and thereby modifying the inner mass-density profile. The resulting density-dependent energy loss competes with heat transport and halo response. An ensemble of initial assembly conditions yields very different final densities at fixed microphysics, although neither a universal constant-density core nor a statistical fit to the observed population is established.
